overview: UNION is a SQL set operator that combines the result sets of two or more SELECT statements into a single result set, stacking rows vertically.
UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result, while UNION ALL keeps every row including duplicates and is therefore faster because it skips the deduplication step.
For UNION/UNION ALL to be valid, every SELECT must return the same number of columns with compatible data types, and a single ORDER BY at the end applies to the entire combined result.
learningObjectives: Understand how UNION combines result sets and how duplicate removal works, including the cost difference versus UNION ALL.
Learn the column-count and data-type compatibility rules and how ORDER BY applies to the whole combined result, not individual SELECTs.
Recognize common use cases for UNION and when to choose UNION ALL for performance.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: UNION is a set operator that returns the union of the rows produced by two or more SELECT statements, eliminating duplicate rows. UNION ALL returns the multiset (bag) union, preserving duplicates. Each operand SELECT must be union-compatible: identical column count and pairwise compatible (coercible) column data types. The column names and types of the overall result are taken from the first SELECT.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: UNION stacks the rows of two queries on top of each other to make one list, and then throws away any exact duplicate rows. UNION ALL does the same stacking but keeps every row, even duplicates. Think of merging two contact lists: UNION gives you one combined list with no repeats, UNION ALL gives you everything including the people who appear in both lists twice.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Set operators UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT trace back to the relational algebra underlying Codd's relational model and were part of SQL from early standards (SQL-86/SQL-92). They directly implement mathematical set union. UNION ALL was provided because true set semantics (dedup) are expensive, and many practical queries combine disjoint sets where deduplication is unnecessary, so the standard offered the cheaper multiset variant.

whyItMatters.business: Combining results from multiple sources or categories into one report (e.g. current plus archived orders) is a routine reporting need that UNION solves directly.
whyItMatters.engineering: UNION lets engineers merge query results from partitioned, sharded, or differently filtered tables into a single uniform result without temporary tables.
whyItMatters.scalability: Choosing UNION ALL when duplicates are impossible avoids an expensive sort/hash deduplication step, which matters greatly on large result sets.
whyItMatters.cost: On scan- or compute-billed warehouses, unnecessary UNION deduplication adds sort/hash cost; using UNION ALL where safe reduces compute and runtime.
whyItMatters.reliability: Understanding compatibility rules prevents subtle bugs where mismatched column order or types silently produce wrong results or runtime errors.

coreComponents.name: Operand SELECT Statements
coreComponents.definition: The two or more SELECT queries whose result sets are combined.
coreComponents.purpose: Each produces a set of rows to be stacked into the combined result.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Must be union-compatible: same column count, compatible data types in matching positions.
coreComponents.examples: SELECT name FROM customers ... UNION ... SELECT name FROM leads ...

coreComponents.name: UNION / UNION ALL Operator
coreComponents.definition: The keyword that joins two SELECTs; UNION deduplicates, UNION ALL preserves duplicates.
coreComponents.purpose: To define whether the combined result removes duplicate rows or keeps all rows.
coreComponents.responsibilities: UNION performs a dedup (sort or hash) across all combined rows; UNION ALL simply concatenates.

coreComponents.name: Final ORDER BY
coreComponents.definition: An optional ORDER BY placed after the last SELECT that sorts the entire combined result.
coreComponents.purpose: To order the unified output; it cannot be attached to individual operand SELECTs.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Sorts the whole result; can reference column names/aliases from the first SELECT or ordinal positions.
coreComponents.examples: SELECT ... UNION SELECT ... ORDER BY name;

internalWorking: The engine executes each operand SELECT and concatenates their output rows into one stream (this alone is UNION ALL).
For UNION, the engine then deduplicates the combined rows by sorting them or building a hash table and discarding exact-duplicate rows across all columns.

Column names and data types of the final result are taken from the first SELECT; values from subsequent SELECTs are implicitly coerced to those types, and a trailing ORDER BY sorts the final combined set.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: SELECT A -> rows A , SELECT B -> rows B -> concatenate (UNION ALL) -> [optional dedup for UNION] -> [optional final ORDER BY] -> single result set
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. SELECT email FROM active_users returns 10,000 emails.
2. SELECT email FROM newsletter_signups returns 4,000 emails, some overlapping with active users.
3. With UNION ALL, all 14,000 rows are returned including overlaps.
4. With UNION, the engine deduplicates, returning only the distinct emails across both sets (e.g. 12,500).
5. A trailing ORDER BY email sorts the final distinct list alphabetically.

keyTerminology.meaning: The requirement that all operand SELECTs return the same number of columns with compatible (coercible) data types in matching positions.
keyTerminology.importance: Violating it causes an error or, worse, silently wrong results when columns are in the wrong order.

keyTerminology.meaning: UNION ALL produces a multiset (duplicates allowed); UNION produces a set (duplicates removed).
keyTerminology.importance: Determines correctness and cost: dedup is needed for set semantics but adds a sort/hash step.

keyTerminology.meaning: The extra sort or hash operation UNION performs to remove duplicates.
keyTerminology.importance: On large results this is the main performance difference between UNION and UNION ALL.

importantConcepts.concept: ORDER BY applies to the whole result
importantConcepts.explanation: You cannot place ORDER BY on an individual operand SELECT (it is only valid on the last SELECT and orders the combined output). To sort within a part before combining, you must use a subquery/derived table, but the final row order is only guaranteed by the trailing ORDER BY.

importantConcepts.concept: Result column names come from the first SELECT
importantConcepts.explanation: The output column names and types are determined by the first SELECT. Subsequent SELECTs' column names are ignored; their values are coerced to the first SELECT's types, so position and type matter more than name.

variationsAndTypes: **UNION:** Combines and removes duplicate rows (set union).
**UNION ALL:** Combines and keeps all rows including duplicates (multiset union), faster.
**INTERSECT:** Returns only rows present in both result sets (set intersection).
**EXCEPT / MINUS:** Returns rows in the first set not in the second (set difference); MINUS is Oracle's spelling.
advantages: **Combines heterogeneous sources:** Merges results from multiple tables or filters into one uniform set.
**Built-in deduplication:** UNION removes duplicates without extra DISTINCT logic.
**Performance control:** UNION ALL avoids dedup cost when duplicates are impossible or acceptable.
**Declarative and portable:** Standard SQL supported across all major databases.
disadvantages: **Dedup overhead:** UNION's sort/hash deduplication is costly on large result sets.
**Strict compatibility rules:** Mismatched column counts or types cause errors or wrong results.
**No per-SELECT ordering:** ORDER BY only applies to the whole result, limiting intermediate sorting.
**Implicit type coercion pitfalls:** Values from later SELECTs are coerced to the first SELECT's types, which can surprise.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use UNION when you need distinct combined rows across sources (deduplicated). Use UNION ALL when the sources are disjoint, duplicates are acceptable, or you will deduplicate later, to avoid the sort/hash cost.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid UNION (use UNION ALL) when you know there are no duplicates, since the dedup is wasted work. Avoid UNION entirely when a JOIN or OR-filter expresses the need more efficiently, or when combining columns horizontally (that is a JOIN, not a UNION).

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: UNION is like merging two guest lists for an event into one master list and crossing off anyone who appears on both, so each person is invited once. UNION ALL is photocopying both lists and stapling them together, keeping every entry even if someone is on both lists twice.

commonMisconceptions.myth: UNION and UNION ALL produce the same result, just at different speeds.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They differ in correctness, not only speed: UNION removes duplicate rows, UNION ALL keeps them. If the sources overlap, the row sets are different.

commonMisconceptions.myth: UNION matches columns by name across SELECTs.
commonMisconceptions.reality: UNION matches columns by position, not name. The first SELECT defines the output names and types; later SELECTs' columns are aligned by order and coerced to those types.

productionConsiderations.scalability: UNION ALL scales linearly as concatenation; UNION adds a sort/hash dedup that grows superlinearly with row count and can spill to disk on large sets. Prefer UNION ALL when duplicates cannot occur.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Enforce union compatibility explicitly by listing columns in the same order and casting types so changes to one table do not silently misalign columns and corrupt results.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: UNION queries run within a single statement and transaction; partial failure rolls back. Large dedup sorts increase memory pressure, so size work memory and use statement timeouts.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch for UNION dedup operations spilling to disk in execution plans on large result sets; these are a common, easily-fixed performance issue (switch to UNION ALL when safe).
productionConsiderations.security: Be cautious that UNION-based combination is also the mechanism behind UNION-based SQL injection; always parameterize queries and never build UNIONs from untrusted input.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: On compute/scan-billed warehouses, replacing UNION with UNION ALL where duplicates are impossible removes a sort step and lowers cost; only deduplicate when business logic requires distinct rows.
productionConsiderations.performance: Push filters into each operand SELECT so each scans less data, ensure operands return matching column projections, and use UNION ALL unless deduplication is genuinely required.

codeExamples.title: UNION ALL vs UNION: combining current and archived orders
codeExamples.overview: Combine live and archived order tables into one result, showing why UNION ALL is correct and faster when the two sources are disjoint.
codeExamples.code:
-- Disjoint sources (no order appears in both) -> use UNION ALL
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, 'current' AS source
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'

UNION ALL

SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount, 'archived' AS source
FROM orders_archive
WHERE order_date < '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY order_id;
codeExamples.breakdown: Both SELECTs return four columns of matching types in the same order. Because an order lives in exactly one of the two tables, there are no duplicates, so UNION ALL is correct and avoids an unnecessary dedup. The literal source column tags each row's origin. The single ORDER BY sorts the entire combined result.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: All current and archived orders in one result set, each tagged 'current' or 'archived', sorted by order_id.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Mismatched column order between the two SELECTs silently misaligns data. Using UNION here would add a needless sort. Placing ORDER BY after the first SELECT is a syntax error.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use UNION ALL because the sources are disjoint. Filter each SELECT by date so each scans only its relevant rows, and index order_date on both tables.

codeExamples.title: UNION for deduplicated contact list across overlapping sources
codeExamples.overview: Build a distinct list of email addresses from customers and newsletter signups, where the same email can appear in both.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT LOWER(email) AS email
FROM customers
WHERE email IS NOT NULL

UNION

SELECT LOWER(email) AS email
FROM newsletter_signups
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY email;
codeExamples.breakdown: Each SELECT normalizes email with LOWER so 'A@x.com' and 'a@x.com' are treated as duplicates. UNION removes duplicate emails across both sources, returning each distinct address once. The trailing ORDER BY sorts the final distinct list.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: An alphabetically sorted list of distinct, lowercased email addresses present in either source, with each address appearing exactly once.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Without LOWER, case differences would survive deduplication. NULL emails would otherwise collapse to one row, hence the IS NOT NULL filters. UNION ALL here would leave duplicates.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: If the two sources were already known to be disjoint, UNION ALL would be cheaper, but since they overlap, the dedup is required. Normalize values before UNION so dedup matches as intended.

codeExamples.title: Combining categorized rows with a label and final sort
codeExamples.overview: Produce a single result that labels customers as 'high value' or 'standard' by unioning two filtered queries, demonstrating ORDER BY over the whole result.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT customer_id, total_spent, 'high_value' AS tier
FROM customer_totals
WHERE total_spent >= 10000

UNION ALL

SELECT customer_id, total_spent, 'standard' AS tier
FROM customer_totals
WHERE total_spent < 10000
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;
codeExamples.breakdown: The two SELECTs partition customers by spend and tag each with a tier label. The partitions are disjoint, so UNION ALL is correct and avoids dedup. The single ORDER BY total_spent DESC sorts the combined high-value and standard rows together.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Every customer in one result, each tagged high_value or standard, sorted by total_spent descending across both tiers.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Attempting ORDER BY inside either SELECT is invalid for the combined result. Using UNION instead of UNION ALL would needlessly attempt deduplication on already-disjoint partitions.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Because the WHERE predicates are mutually exclusive, UNION ALL is the correct and faster choice. Reference the alias total_spent (from the first SELECT) in ORDER BY.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A retailer stores recent transactions in a hot orders table and older ones in an orders_archive table. Finance needs a single year-to-date revenue report that spans both tables, with each row labeled by source, sorted for review.
endToEndExample.inputData: Two tables, orders and orders_archive, with identical relevant columns (order_id, customer_id, amount, order_date). An order exists in exactly one table.
endToEndExample.architecture: A single query that UNION ALLs a filtered SELECT from orders with a filtered SELECT from orders_archive, projecting matching columns plus a source label, finished with one ORDER BY over the combined result.
processingSteps: 1. SELECT relevant columns and a 'current' label from orders filtered to the current period.
2. SELECT the same columns and an 'archived' label from orders_archive filtered to prior periods.
3. Combine the two with UNION ALL because the sources are disjoint (no duplicates possible).
4. Apply a single ORDER BY over the combined result for the report.
5. Optionally aggregate the unioned result in an outer query for total revenue.
endToEndExample.output: A unified result set of all in-scope orders from both the live and archived tables, each tagged with its source, sorted as required, with no duplicate rows because the sources do not overlap.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Review the execution plan to confirm no unnecessary dedup/sort step is introduced, and that each operand uses an index on order_date rather than a full scan.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Validate that both SELECTs project identical column counts and compatible types; a schema change to one table that adds/removes a column would break union compatibility and must be caught in CI.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A correct, efficient combined revenue dataset built with UNION ALL (avoiding wasted deduplication), giving finance a single sorted view across hot and archived data that can be aggregated or exported.

industryUseCases.company: Retail / finance reporting (e.g. combining hot and archived data)
industryUseCases.problem: Reporting must span a live transactions table and an archived table that together cover the full history.
industryUseCases.solution: UNION ALL the filtered live and archived SELECTs (disjoint sources) into one result for reporting.
industryUseCases.benefits: Single uniform report across storage tiers with no duplicate rows and no dedup overhead.

industryUseCases.company: Marketing / CRM platforms (e.g. unified contact lists)
industryUseCases.problem: Building a deduplicated audience from overlapping sources such as customers, leads, and newsletter signups.
industryUseCases.solution: UNION the normalized email/identity columns from each source to produce one distinct contact list.
industryUseCases.benefits: A clean, deduplicated audience for campaigns, avoiding emailing the same person twice.

industryUseCases.company: Analytics over partitioned/sharded data (e.g. per-region tables)
industryUseCases.problem: Data is split across per-region or per-month tables that must be analyzed together.
industryUseCases.solution: UNION ALL the per-partition SELECTs (disjoint by design) into one result set for analysis.
industryUseCases.benefits: Cross-partition analysis without physically merging tables, with no wasted deduplication.

productionDeepDive.scalability: UNION ALL scales as simple concatenation and parallelizes well; UNION adds a global deduplication (sort or hash) whose cost grows with result size and can spill to disk. At scale, prefer UNION ALL whenever duplicates are impossible by construction.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: UNION queries are single statements with normal transactional rollback. The main risk is memory pressure from large dedup sorts; mitigate with adequate work memory and statement timeouts.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: No special HA concerns; UNION queries can run on read replicas. Combining per-shard SELECTs is a common pattern for querying horizontally partitioned data.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: UNION produces no persisted artifact; only the underlying tables matter for backup and restore. Cross-table UNION reports must be validated after restore if tables are recovered independently.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use UNION ALL unless deduplication is required. Push selective WHERE predicates into each operand so each scans minimal data, ensure matching projections, index operand filter/sort columns, and verify the plan does not add a redundant sort.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: On compute/scan-billed engines, removing an unnecessary UNION dedup step directly lowers cost. Deduplicate only when business logic needs distinct rows; otherwise UNION ALL is both correct and cheaper.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: UNION is the basis of UNION-based SQL injection, where an attacker appends a UNION SELECT to exfiltrate data. Always use parameterized queries, validate input, and never concatenate untrusted strings into SQL containing UNION.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Flag UNION queries whose dedup sort spills to disk and review whether UNION ALL would be correct. Track runtime and memory of large set-operator queries over time.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Confirm operand SELECTs stay union-compatible (column count/types) as schemas evolve; add tests so a column added to one source table does not silently break or misalign the UNION.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log slow set-operator queries and alert on dedup spills or runtime regressions, which often indicate an avoidable UNION-instead-of-UNION-ALL choice or a growing result set.

recommendedPractices: **Use UNION ALL by default** and only use UNION when deduplication is genuinely required, to avoid the sort/hash cost.
**List explicit columns in the same order** in every operand SELECT to guarantee correct alignment.
**Cast columns to matching types** where coercion is ambiguous so the first SELECT's types are intentional.
**Place a single ORDER BY at the very end** to sort the whole combined result.
engineeringStandards: Never combine result sets that differ in column count or incompatible types; enforce union compatibility in code review and CI.
Add a literal source/tier column when the origin of each row matters for downstream logic.
Avoid building UNIONs from untrusted input to eliminate UNION-based injection risk.
designRecommendations: Prefer a JOIN over UNION when you are combining columns horizontally rather than stacking rows vertically.
When sources are disjoint by design (partitions, hot/cold tiers), use UNION ALL and document why duplicates cannot occur.
Normalize values (case, trimming) before UNION so deduplication matches as intended.
namingConventions: Use the same aliases across operand SELECTs so the first SELECT's output names are meaningful.
Name the origin column source or tier consistently.
Reference the first SELECT's column aliases (not later ones) in the trailing ORDER BY.
documentationStandards: Document why UNION ALL vs UNION was chosen (disjoint sources vs need for distinct rows).
Note the expected column mapping across operands when projections are non-trivial.
Record any implicit type coercions so future schema changes do not break alignment.
testingStrategies: Test with overlapping data to confirm UNION deduplicates and UNION ALL preserves duplicates as intended.
Add a test that fails if operand column counts or types diverge after a schema change.
Verify the final ORDER BY sorts across the whole combined result, not just one operand.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using UNION when UNION ALL would be correct and faster.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers default to UNION out of habit, not realizing it triggers an expensive deduplication.
commonMistakes.impact: Unnecessary sort/hash work on large result sets, slower queries, and higher compute cost, with no change in results when sources are already disjoint.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use UNION ALL whenever duplicates cannot occur or are acceptable; reserve UNION for when distinct rows are required.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mismatched column order or types between operand SELECTs.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Operands are written separately and columns drift out of alignment, especially with SELECT *.
commonMistakes.impact: Either an error, or silently wrong results where, for example, a city value lands in a name column due to positional matching.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: List explicit columns in identical order and compatible types in every operand; avoid SELECT * in UNION queries.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to ORDER BY (or LIMIT) inside an individual operand SELECT for the whole result.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Expecting each SELECT to sort its own part of the combined output.
commonMistakes.impact: Syntax error in most engines, or the order is not preserved through the UNION, giving an unordered final result.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Place a single ORDER BY after the last SELECT; to limit a part before combining, wrap that part in a derived table.

comparisonSection.explanation: UNION removes duplicate rows by performing a sort or hash dedup across the combined result, which adds cost that grows with size. UNION ALL simply concatenates rows and keeps duplicates, making it faster. They differ in results, not just speed, when the sources overlap; choose based on whether distinct rows are required.

UNION stacks rows vertically from result sets with the same columns. A JOIN combines columns horizontally by matching rows on a key. If you need to add columns from a related table, use a JOIN; if you need to append rows from a similar query, use UNION/UNION ALL.

UNION returns rows in either set (deduplicated). INTERSECT returns rows present in both sets, and EXCEPT (MINUS in Oracle) returns rows in the first set but not the second. All require union-compatible operands; pick the operator matching the set logic you need.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Both combine the rows of two or more SELECTs into one result set with matching columns. UNION removes duplicate rows by performing a deduplication step, while UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates and is therefore faster because it skips deduplication.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: State that the difference is correctness (dedup vs not) plus the resulting performance cost. Mention they differ in output when sources overlap.

beginnerQuestions.question: What rules must the SELECT statements in a UNION satisfy?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Each SELECT must return the same number of columns, and the columns in matching positions must have compatible (coercible) data types. Columns are matched by position, not by name, and the output column names and types come from the first SELECT.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize union compatibility and that matching is positional, which is a common interview gotcha.

intermediateQuestions.question: Where can ORDER BY go in a UNION query and what does it sort?
intermediateQuestions.answer: ORDER BY can only appear once, after the final SELECT, and it sorts the entire combined result set. You cannot attach an ORDER BY to an individual operand SELECT to order the whole output; to order or limit a part before combining, you must wrap that part in a derived table.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Tests understanding that the set operators produce one logical result and ordering applies globally.

intermediateQuestions.question: When should you prefer UNION ALL over UNION, and why does it matter for performance?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Prefer UNION ALL when the operand result sets are disjoint, when duplicates are acceptable, or when you will deduplicate later. It matters because UNION must sort or hash the combined rows to remove duplicates, which is expensive on large sets and can spill to disk, whereas UNION ALL just concatenates.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Connect the choice to the dedup sort/hash cost and to correctness when sources do not overlap.

advancedQuestions.question: A report uses UNION across two large disjoint tables and is slow. How do you speed it up without changing results?
advancedQuestions.answer: Since the tables are disjoint, switching UNION to UNION ALL removes the unnecessary deduplication sort/hash with identical results, which is usually the biggest win. Additionally, push selective WHERE predicates into each operand so each scans less data, ensure both operands project the same columns, index the filter/sort columns, and verify the plan no longer contains a redundant sort step.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Shows you can identify the wasted dedup and apply standard scan-reduction and plan-verification techniques.

advancedQuestions.question: How does UNION relate to SQL injection, and how do you prevent it?
advancedQuestions.answer: UNION-based injection appends a malicious UNION SELECT to a vulnerable query to read data from other tables (matching column count and types). Prevent it by using parameterized queries / prepared statements, never concatenating untrusted input into SQL, applying least-privilege database accounts, and validating input. The defense is the same as for SQL injection generally.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Tests security awareness around set operators and the standard parameterization defense.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: You need one alphabetical list of all distinct cities that appear in either a customers table or a suppliers table.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Both sources have a city column. The same city can appear in both, and within each table, so distinct rows are required. Use UNION (which deduplicates) and a final ORDER BY. Normalize case if needed.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: SELECT city FROM customers UNION SELECT city FROM suppliers ORDER BY city; UNION removes duplicate cities across and within both sources; the trailing ORDER BY sorts the distinct combined list. Use UNION (not UNION ALL) because deduplication is required.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a query layer that presents a unified transaction history over data split into hot (recent) and cold (archived) tables, with low latency and correct results.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Expose a view that UNION ALLs the hot and cold tables, since each transaction lives in exactly one tier (disjoint), avoiding deduplication. Filter each operand by the time range so only the relevant tier is scanned for a given query.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: UNION ALL is correct and cheap because sources are disjoint; using UNION would add needless dedup cost. The trade-off is that the view must be kept union-compatible as schemas evolve, and queries must push time filters into both operands to avoid scanning the wrong tier.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Partition or index both tables on the time column so each operand scan is bounded, serve the view from read replicas, and ensure the optimizer prunes the archived operand when a query targets only recent data. Add CI checks that both tables remain column-compatible.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: UNION stacks the rows of two or more union-compatible SELECTs into one result set and removes duplicates; UNION ALL does the same but keeps duplicates and is faster.
keyConcepts: Union compatibility: same column count, compatible types, matched by position.
UNION = dedup (sort/hash); UNION ALL = concatenate, keep duplicates.
Output names/types come from the first SELECT.
A single trailing ORDER BY sorts the whole combined result.
UNION is vertical (rows); JOIN is horizontal (columns).
commands: SELECT a, b FROM t1 UNION SELECT a, b FROM t2 ORDER BY a;
SELECT a, b FROM t1 UNION ALL SELECT a, b FROM t2;
SELECT a FROM t1 INTERSECT SELECT a FROM t2;
SELECT a FROM t1 EXCEPT SELECT a FROM t2;  -- MINUS in Oracle
interviewPoints: UNION removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps them (correctness + speed).
Columns matched by position, not name; types from first SELECT.
ORDER BY only at the end, applies to the whole result.
Prefer UNION ALL on disjoint sources to skip dedup cost.
UNION is the basis of UNION-based SQL injection - parameterize.
quickNotes: Every operand SELECT must return the same number of columns with compatible types.
Use UNION ALL by default; use UNION only when distinct rows are required.
Wrap an operand in a derived table to ORDER BY or LIMIT it before combining.
Avoid SELECT * in UNION queries to prevent positional misalignment.
INTERSECT = rows in both; EXCEPT/MINUS = rows in first but not second.

keyTakeaways: UNION combines the rows of two or more SELECTs and removes duplicates, while UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster because it skips the deduplication sort/hash - they differ in results, not just speed, when sources overlap.
Operands must be union-compatible: the same number of columns with compatible types, matched by position (not name), with output names and types taken from the first SELECT.
A single ORDER BY at the end sorts the entire combined result; you cannot order an individual operand for the whole output without a derived table.
Prefer UNION ALL whenever duplicates are impossible (disjoint sources like hot/cold tiers or partitions) to avoid wasted deduplication cost, reserving UNION for when distinct rows are required.
UNION stacks rows vertically (unlike a JOIN, which combines columns horizontally) and underlies UNION-based SQL injection, so always parameterize queries built around it.
